overview: Nomingia (named after the Nomingiin Gobi, a region of southern Mongolia) was a caenagnathid oviraptorosaurian theropod from the Late Cretaceous (Maastrichtian, approximately 72–66 million years ago). Fossils come from the Nemegt Formation of Omnogovi Aimag, Mongolia. With an estimated length around 1.6 metres, it was a moderately small oviraptorosaur with an omnivorous diet and ground-dwelling habits.

Described by Barsbold, Osmólska, Watabe, Currie and Tsogtbaatar in 2000, Nomingia is scientifically notable for preserving a pygostyle — a fused terminal series of tail vertebrae previously known only in birds and closely related avialans. This discovery provided direct evidence that at least some non-avian oviraptorosaurs bore fan-shaped tail feathers, profoundly influencing understanding of the evolution of tail plumage in the theropod lineage.

articles.title: Discovery and Naming
articles.body: Nomingia gobiensis was described in 2000 by a team led by Rinchen Barsbold and including Halszka Osmólska, Mahito Watabe, Philip Currie and Khishigjav Tsogtbaatar. The holotype is a partial postcranial skeleton lacking the skull, found in the Nemegt Formation. The genus name refers to the Nomingiin Gobi Desert locality.

articles.title: The Pygostyle Discovery
articles.body: The most significant anatomical feature of Nomingia is its pygostyle — the last several caudal vertebrae are co-ossified into a single plate-like structure. Until the description of Nomingia, pygostyles were known only in birds and Caudipteryx. The presence of a pygostyle in Nomingia, a caenagnathid, suggests that fan-shaped tail feathers evolved independently in oviraptorosaurs or were present in the common ancestor of oviraptorosaurs and birds.

articles.title: Diet and Ecology
articles.body: Caenagnathids and their relatives among oviraptorosaurs are generally considered omnivores, with robust beaks capable of processing a variety of food items including seeds, invertebrates, eggs and small vertebrates. PBDB ecospace data classifies Nomingia as omnivorous. It inhabited the Nemegt river-plain ecosystem alongside large theropods, hadrosaurs and sauropods.

articles.title: Taxonomic and Phylogenetic Position
articles.body: Nomingia is placed within Caenagnathinae within Caenagnathidae, a North American and Asian clade of oviraptorosaurs. Caenagnathids are distinguished from oviraptorids by features of the pelvis and hindlimb. The phylogenetic placement of Nomingia has been largely stable since its description, consistently recovering it as a derived caenagnathid.

record.taxonomicStatus: probable junior synonym of Elmisaurus rarus
record.description: Nomingia gobiensis was named for a partial oviraptorosaur skeleton from the Nemegt Formation, notable for fused terminal tail vertebrae. A 2021 revision found it most likely to be the same taxon as Elmisaurus rarus.
facts: The holotype lacks a skull but preserves vertebral, pelvic and limb material.
Its short fused tail tip is real, though calling it identical to a modern bird pygostyle can overstate convergence.
This page should be retained as a historical synonym rather than counted as a separate accepted genus.

review.ageReviewNote: The specimen is from the Maastrichtian Nemegt Formation, not merely a generic 72-68 Ma range.
